items.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019
items.q: And there was an opening of an exhibit on Count Basie and I brought my little — at that time I had a hand-held cassette machine that was about this big, you remember, that you press the button like this, and I remember bringing it in and I tape recorded on a cassette the first opening night. And it

ctx.x: All right. I consider myself pretty lucky too. And at one point I had had, because I was in the right place at the right time I got to ride to a gig with the Statesmen of Jazz, and like Milt Hinton was on my left, and he fell asleep on my shoulder. And I’m thinking, this is Milt Hinton and I’m with him, and Panama Francis and Claude Williams, and I’m just like, said to myself, you should really take note of this and appreciate it. So I’m wondering if you had that same feeling. You played beside, you know, Eddie…

To the degree that a 19-year-old can, or a 25-year-old. Yeah. I mean if you want to work biographically up to how all those things happened, so I’m back in New Jersey, you know, and I’m a teenager, and my parents are meeting some of these people and I’m hearing Teddy Wilson and then Hank Jones also was playing solo piano at a place called the Sherry Netherlands and I used to go there. My parents would leave me and Hank would drive me home. Was I appreciating it as to what it really was? How could I? I was 16…

friends with Bobby Hackett and he was like an adopted son of Louis’s, of Louis Armstrong, and a lifelong disciple of his. And he wound up becoming the manager of this small little jazz museum. And he took me on as a volunteer. So every Saturday and Sunday I would take the bus — you could take a bus from suburban New Jersey into New York, it was easy, and my parents let me do it, unbelievable. And I wound up volunteering there for years. And this is where I got to know Marge Singleton, Zutty Singleton’s wife, it’s…
